title: How would you replace a legacy service without a big-bang migration — find a boundary where traffic or responsibility can move incrementally (a strangler-fig pattern, a compatibility layer, shadow traffic, parallel validation, or consumer-by-consumer cutover) — and why must the design include how the organization RETURNS to the previous state when the new path misbehaves?
shortTitle: How would you replace a legacy service without a big-bang migration?

s1_definition.profdef: Replacing a legacy service without a big-bang rewrite means moving traffic or responsibility to the new implementation incrementally while the old one keeps serving the rest. The enabling idea is the strangler-fig pattern: you place a facade or router in front of the legacy service and route a slice of traffic — one endpoint, one capability, one consumer, or a small percentage — to the new service, growing that slice over time until the legacy service handles nothing and can be retired. Supporting techniques include a compatibility layer that translates between old and new contracts, shadow traffic that sends real requests to the new service without using its responses so you can compare behaviour safely, parallel validation that runs both and flags divergence, and consumer-by-consumer cutover. Critically, the design must include an explicit, fast path back to the old service for every increment, because incremental migration is only safe if each step is reversible the moment the new path misbehaves.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to replace its decades-old transaction system, but it cannot switch everything over one night and hope — if it fails, the whole bank stops. So instead they put a receptionist (a router) in front. At first the receptionist sends every request to the old system, exactly as before. Then they quietly start sending just balance enquiries to the new system while everything else still goes to the old one, and they double-check the new answers against the old. If balance enquiries work well for a week, they move cheque deposits too, then transfers, one capability at a time, each time keeping the old system ready. The strangler fig grows around the old tree branch by branch until the old tree is fully replaced and can be cut down. And at every step the receptionist can instantly send that traffic back to the old system if the new one gives a wrong answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put a router in front of the legacy service and move one capability or slice at a time to the new one — validating in parallel and keeping an instant path back — until the legacy is strangled and retired.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a legacy monolithic account service handles balance enquiries, transfers, and statements. The team is building a new account service and must replace the legacy one without downtime or a risky big-bang switch.

Problem 1 — a big-bang cutover would move all three capabilities at once with no gradual learning, and if transfers broke, the bank would be down with no quick way back.

Problem 2 — the new service must be proven against real traffic before it is trusted, and each capability must move independently with an instant path back.

The fix uses a strangler facade that routes per capability, starts with the read-only balance enquiry, shadows the new service against the legacy and compares responses, cuts balance enquiry over by percentage once divergence is zero, and keeps a feature flag to route instantly back to legacy. The mini-project builds a `StranglerFacade`, a `LegacyAccountService`, a `NewAccountService`, a shadow-and-compare step, and a `FeatureFlags` toggle, and the demo shows balance enquiry shadowed, cut over, then rolled back instantly on a simulated divergence while transfers remain on legacy throughout.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: balance-enquiry, transfer, and statement requests, with the new service initially only handling balance enquiry.

Step 1 — Shadow balance enquiry. Request R1 for balance enquiry goes to the facade in shadow mode. The facade calls the legacy service, which returns the balance, and also calls the new service, compares the two responses, finds they match, and returns the legacy response to the caller. The new service was exercised on real traffic with zero customer risk.

Step 2 — Cut balance enquiry over. With divergence at zero, the team enables the new service for balance enquiry. Request R2 now routes to the new service, which returns the correct balance. Only this one capability moved.

Step 3 — Transfers stay on legacy. Request R3 for a transfer routes to the legacy service, because transfer was never migrated. The migration is strictly incremental: one capability at a time, the rest untouched.

Step 4 — A bug appears, divergence detected. A bug is injected into the new service so it returns a wrong balance. Request R4 in shadow mode shows the legacy and new responses disagree, and the facade logs a divergence warning. Parallel validation caught the problem.

Step 5 — Instant rollback. The team flips the feature flag to route balance enquiry back to legacy. Request R5 now routes to the legacy service again and returns the correct balance. The rollback was instant, lost no data because both read from the shared source of truth, and never touched transfers. The strangler pattern let the team learn, cut over, and retreat safely, all per capability.

```
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [INFO] === Shadow phase: balance-enquiry ===
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [INFO] Cutover: balance=1000000.00
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [INFO] Routing transfer to LEGACY service
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [INFO] Transfer stays legacy: transfer=OK
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [WARNING] DIVERGENCE R4: legacy=balance=1000000.00 new=balance=999999.99
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [WARNING] Divergence detected → instant rollback of balance-enquiry to legacy
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [INFO] Routing balance-enquiry to LEGACY service
2026-10-24 19:28:02 [INFO] After rollback: balance=1000000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Callers (unchanged) → StranglerFacade (router in front of legacy)
    │
    ├─ balance-enquiry
    │   SHADOW: legacy ✓ returned, new compared (no impact)
    │   divergence 0 → CUTOVER: route to NEW (ramp %)
    │   bug/divergence → FLIP FLAG → back to LEGACY (instant, no data loss)
    ├─ transfer   → LEGACY (not migrated yet)
    └─ statement  → LEGACY (not migrated yet)
    ▼
  Legacy strangled capability-by-capability; retire only when it serves nothing.
  Shared source of truth → rollback never loses data.
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Incremental, Reversible Cutover ═══

  ┌─ Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strangler-Fig: facade routes a growing slice to new        │
  │ Shadow Traffic + Parallel Validation: compare before trust │
  │ Compatibility Layer: translate old↔new contracts           │
  │ Feature Flag: instant per-capability rollback              │

  │ S: Facade routes; Legacy/New handle; Flags decide          │
  │ O: migrate a new capability = flip a flag, no rewrite       │
  │ D: Facade depends on a handler abstraction, not concretes   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────┐ uses ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ StranglerFacade  │─────▶│ LegacyAccountService │
  │ + shadow()       │─────▶│ NewAccountService    │
  │ + route()        │─────▶│ FeatureFlags         │
  └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a capability's migration ──
  [LEGACY] ──shadow, 0 divergence──→ [CUTOVER (ramp %)] ──stable──→ [NEW ONLY]

  ── Call Chain (rollback) ──
  1. facade.shadow(R4, balance-enquiry) → divergence logged
  2. flags.rollbackToLegacy("balance-enquiry")
  3. facade.route(R5) → legacy.handle → correct balance
  4. transfers untouched throughout
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I would never replace a legacy service with a big-bang rewrite, because that concentrates all the risk into a single switch-over moment with no gradual learning and often no safe way back. Instead I use the strangler-fig pattern, which spreads the risk across many small, reversible steps. I put a routing facade in front of the legacy service so that from the callers' perspective nothing changes — they call the same address — and behind the facade I decide per request where it goes, starting with everything on legacy and progressively moving slices to the new service. The first job is to find a clean boundary to split on: a single endpoint, a bounded capability like balance enquiry, a specific consumer, or a traffic percentage, and I pick the smallest, lowest-risk slice first, ideally a read-only operation, so a mistake there is cheap.

Before I ever trust the new service, I de-risk with shadow traffic and parallel validation. Shadow traffic means the facade sends the real request to both the legacy and the new service, returns the legacy response to the customer, and discards the new one — but logs and compares them. That exercises the new service under genuine production load and data with zero customer impact. Parallel validation flags any divergence between the two responses, so I discover behavioural differences before the new service is ever authoritative. Only when divergence is zero and confidence is high do I cut that slice over, usually ramping by percentage so I can watch the metrics at each step, and a compatibility layer translates any contract differences so callers do not have to change in lockstep. Then I repeat for the next slice until the legacy service serves nothing and can be retired.

The part I would emphasise most is the return path, because that is what makes incremental migration genuinely safe rather than a big-bang in disguise. Every increment must include a designed, fast, rehearsed way back to the legacy service — in practice a feature flag or routing rule I can flip instantly — plus the guarantee that the legacy service is still fully functional and its data is still current. That usually means writes go to a shared source of truth or are dual-written during the migration, so flipping back never loses data. I treat "how do we get back" as a first-class requirement of each step, and I test the rollback before the cutover, because discovering mid-incident that there is no safe way back is exactly the failure the pattern exists to prevent.

In my banking work this was how we replaced a legacy account service. We put a facade in front, shadowed balance enquiry first and compared every response against legacy, cut it over by percentage once divergence was zero, and left transfers and statements on legacy until their turn. When a bug later made the new balance diverge, we flipped the flag and routed balance enquiry straight back to legacy instantly, losing no data because both read from the shared store, and transfers were never affected. The principle I take into interviews is that a legacy replacement succeeds not when the new service is built, but when every increment is small, validated in parallel, and individually reversible, so the organisation can always walk back to the previous state the moment the new path misbehaves.
